query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under high-temperature operation, the stability of solid‐solution high‐entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles is governed by temperature‐activated atomic diffusion that drives element segregation and phase transformation, but this process is significantly accelerated by reactive catalytic atmospheres (e.g., H2-rich) compared to inert thermoelectric conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios, crystallized as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Heat the nanoparticles from 473 K to 1923 K under two different environments—one set in a catalytic (e.g., hydrogen-containing) atmosphere and another in an inert or vacuum (thermoelectric) atmosphere.
generation.conditions: In situ experiments using high-temperature synchrotron X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy with controlled atmosphere conditions, ensuring identical heating rates and holding times.
generation.structural_mediator: Temperature-activated atomic diffusion leading to differential mobilities among constituent metals and resultant local chemical segregation.
generation.mechanism: Reactive catalytic atmospheres promote reduction or differential chemical reactivity among metals, thereby lowering the activation barrier for atomic diffusion and triggering selective segregation and phase transformation. In contrast, inert conditions limit such promoted diffusion, preserving the high-entropy solid solution structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under catalytic conditions, in situ measurements will show the onset of phase segregation or the formation of secondary phases (local compositional heterogeneities) at high temperatures, while under inert conditions, the nanoparticles will largely retain their uniform solid-solution structure even at 1923 K.
generation.baseline: The as-synthesized state of uniformly mixed HEA nanoparticles obtained at room temperature.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under heating regimes from 473 K to 1923 K and for nanoparticles prepared as homogeneous HEAs. It may not hold if particle size, support material, or non-equiatomic compositions introduce additional kinetic or thermodynamic effects.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperatures at which segregation initiates and the degree of phase transformation may vary depending on specific metal compositions and particle sizes; further quantitative analysis is needed for precise thresholds.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ high-temperature synchrotron XRD and TEM analyses of HEA nanoparticles while heating from 473 K to 1923 K under both hydrogen-rich (catalytic) and inert atmospheres. Monitor phase evolution and elemental distribution in real time.
measurements: XRD patterns for phase identification and lattice parameter changes
TEM and elemental mapping to assess compositional homogeneity or segregation
EXAFS to probe local bonding environments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the comparative analysis shows similar phase behavior and retention of a homogeneous solid solution under both catalytic and inert conditions, with no significant signs of element segregation or secondary phase formation at high temperatures, then the hypothesis that reactive atmospheres promote accelerated segregation would be falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:Synthesis and characterization of HEA nanoparticles
cited_evidence.text: The CoMoFeNiCu HEA nanoparticles were synthesized by employing flash heating and cooling of metal precursors on oxygenated carbon supports, with the temperature going up to 2000–2300 K, the temperature ramping rate on the order of 105 K s−1 and the duration of shocks as short as ~55 ms (Fig. 2a–c). Under such conditions, the high temperature induced rapid thermal-decomposition of the precursors, forming small liquid droplets of multimetallic solutions. The subsequent rapid cooling enabled crystallization of these liquid droplets into uniform and homogeneous alloy nanoparticles without being subjected to aggregation/agglomeration, element segregation or phase separation. Five types of HEA nanoparticles with the general composition CoxMoyFe10Ni10Cu10 (x + y = 70) were prepared by using this method, in which the atomic ratio of Co/Mo was controlled to be 15/55, 25/45, 35/35, 45/25, and 55/15 by varying the loading of precursors, the overall loading of metals in each catalyst was controlled at 10 wt% during synthesis. These nanoparticles are denoted as HEA-CoxMoy (e.g., HEA-Co15Mo55 for Co15Mo55Fe10Ni10Cu10) in the following discussion. Bimetallic Co-Mo and monometallic Ru nanoparticle

The stability of the MEA-NPs is critical for their practical application at elevated temperatures. We, therefore, performed an in situ stability test in the electron microscope from room temperature up to 873 K, annealing the NPs at each test point for at least 30 min. As shown in Fig. 4A, the ultrafine Ru-5 MEA-NPs maintain their uniform dispersion throughout the in situ tests up to 873 K and demonstrate superior size stability after high-temperature annealing. In addition, the NPs are still in a homogeneous alloy structure without elemental segregation or phase separation (Fig. 4B), showing their structural stability. Note that the Co and Ni after annealing are slightly less than the nominal composition, which is likely due to metal evaporation at high temperature in the microscope vacuum. We also confirmed the alloy structure macroscopically by powder and synchrotron x-ray diffraction, showing a single-phase fcc structure with a fitted lattice constant of 3.673 Å (fig. S3, B and C).

Nanoparticles with a range of sizes and morphologies have been extensively studied for various catalytic applications; however, most nanoparticles studied comprise three or fewer elements to avoid synthetic complexity and structural heterogeneity (). Multimetallic nanoclusters (MMNCs; i.e., ultrafine nanoparticles with ≥3 elements) represent a vast and largely undiscovered chemical space that promised to tune material properties via high-dimensional composition control and the associated synergistic interactions among different elements (). However, with increasing compositional complexity, conventional synthetic methods often lead to MMNCs with wider size distribution and inhomogeneous structures (e.g., phase separation and/or elemental segregation inside the particles). These inhomogeneities originate from the substantial challenge in controlling the kinetics and dynamics of chemical reactions at the nanoscale among these dissimilar constituents (, , , , ). chosen.conditions: Under carefully regulated catalytic (e.g., H2-rich) and thermoelectric (e.g., inert) environments while ramping from 473 K to 1923 K, starting from well-characterized solid solution nanoparticles.
chosen.why: This approach directly tests the mechanistic hypothesis that high-temperature stability of these multi-metal nanoparticles is governed by thermally activated element segregation and phase transformation processes. By controlling temperature and reactive atmospheres and performing in situ structural and chemical analyses, the study fills the niche by comparing the operational behavior directly against the as-synthesized baseline. The controlled variable experiment is a standard and robust method in materials science for dissecting mechanisms under operational conditions.
